148.title: Ash Wednesday (Genesis 3:19)
148.hook: ashes on the forehead: dust thou art, and into dust thou shalt return
148.howItsDone: On Ash Wednesday Catholics go to church to receive a cross of ashes on the forehead, often wearing it through the day, and those old enough fast and abstain from meat.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ordinary Time: not plain weeks, but counted ones. Your line was green, growing.

One Wednesday in late winter, people around town have a dark smudge on their foreheads. The barista. A nurse on her lunch break. A guy on the subway. Someone at work leans over: you've got something on your face. They know. It's on purpose. Catholics aren't required to go to Mass that day, and still the lines form, to hear something people spend a lot of effort not thinking about. Today: Ash Wednesday.
screen: `A SMUDGE ON THE FOREHEAD.` → `YOU'VE GOT SOMETHING ON YOUR FACE.` → `THEY KNOW.`

segments.voice: Ash Wednesday is the first day of Lent, the season that leads to Easter. The ashes traditionally come from burning the palm branches of the previous year's Palm Sunday, so last spring's celebration becomes this spring's dust. The priest, deacon or minister dips a thumb in the ashes, traces a cross on each forehead, and says one of two sentences. One is from the Gospel of Mark: "repent, and believe the gospel." The other, the traditional one, comes from Genesis, when God speaks to Adam after the fall. In the Douay-Rheims: "for dust thou art, and into dust thou shalt return." In the old Latin: Memento, homo, quia pulvis es, et in pulverem reverteris. Remember, man, that you are dust. That sounds grim at first. But in Genesis, God forms the first human out of the dust of the ground and breathes life into him. Dust isn't an insult. It's what people are made of, and what God chose to breathe into. So, as Catholics read it, the ashes say two things at once. You are going to die. And, in the Genesis story, you are dust that God shaped by hand and filled with breath. Dust, and loved. Catholics between eighteen and fifty-nine fast that day, one full meal and two small ones, and everyone fourteen and older skips meat. The day isn't morbid. It's honest. Life is short, and knowing it plainly can make you kinder, braver, less hurried about things that don't matter. Other Christians keep it too: Anglicans, Lutherans, Methodists and more.

segments.voice: Touch your forehead lightly with your thumb, where the ashes would go, and let yourself think it: one day, I'll die; don't rush past it, and don't spiral. Then feel your breath going in and out, the breath Genesis says God gave. If you pray, say dust, and loved; if you don't, let the plain fact make the next hour a little gentler.
Ash Wednesday. The first day of Lent, a cross of ashes on the forehead, and the words: dust thou art. Today's word.
Your line: dust, and loved. Both are true at once, ashes and breath. See you tomorrow.

149.title: Prayer, fasting, almsgiving (Matthew 6:1–18)
149.hook: Lent's three practices, done in secret
149.howItsDone: In Lent Catholics take up prayer, fasting and almsgiving, often giving up something, adding a practice, and putting what they save into a parish collection box for the poor, given at Easter.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ash Wednesday: dust thou art. Your line was dust, and loved.

You've seen it online. Someone posts a photo from the soup kitchen, well lit, with a caption about giving back. Someone else announces they're on day three of a fast. Someone's been up since five for prayer. None of it is bad. But something about it is odd, and Jesus named it long before phones. On Ash Wednesday, the Gospel at Catholic Mass is his answer: three practices, and one condition. Today: almsgiving, and its two companions.
screen: `A WELL-LIT PHOTO OF GIVING.` → `DAY THREE OF A FAST.` → `THREE PRACTICES, ONE CONDITION.`

segments.voice: In the Sermon on the Mount, in Matthew chapter six, Jesus takes the three great religious practices of his own Jewish tradition, giving to the poor, prayer and fasting, and says the same thing about each: don't do it to be seen. Do it in secret. On giving, in the Douay-Rheims: "But when thou dost alms, let not thy left hand know what thy right hand doth." On prayer: "But thou when thou shalt pray, enter into thy chamber, and having shut the door, pray to thy Father in secret." On fasting: wash your face and look normal, so no one can tell. Each time the promise is the same: your Father who sees in secret will repay you. These three became the backbone of Lent. Prayer turns you toward God. Fasting turns you away from your own appetites. Almsgiving turns you toward your neighbor. Alms comes, through Latin, from the Greek eleemosyne, mercy. Giving alms is doing mercy, and Catholics count more than money here: time, attention, a meal, a visit, patience. Some parishes hand out a small cardboard box at the start of Lent, and families drop in what they save by eating simply, to be given away at Easter. Why secret? The moment you do good in order to be seen, the audience becomes the point. Jesus calls that having your reward already. Done in secret, the good deed stays pointed at God and at the person you're helping. And there's a freedom in it: nobody's watching, so you don't have to perform. Tomorrow, a walk around the church walls.

segments.voice: Pick one of the three: a few quiet minutes of prayer, door shut; a small fast, skipping a snack, a scroll or a second coffee; or one act of mercy nobody will know about, money, time or a kind word. Picture yourself doing it, and decide you won't mention it to anyone. If you pray, you can offer it to God.

150.title: The Stations of the Cross
150.hook: fourteen stops from condemnation to the tomb
150.howItsDone: Catholics pray the Stations of the Cross especially on Fridays in Lent, walking or turning from station to station around the church, with a reading, a reflection and a prayer at each.

segments.voice: Yesterday, almsgiving and Lent's three practices, all done in secret. Your line was in secret.

Fourteen small pictures or carvings hang along the side walls of many Catholic churches, evenly spaced, each with a little cross above it and a Roman numeral underneath. Most weeks nobody pays them much attention. But on Friday evenings in Lent, the lights dim and a small group gathers at the first one. They stand. They kneel. They move to the next. Slowly they walk the walls of the church, all the way around, until they end at the tomb.
screen: `FOURTEEN PICTURES ON THE WALLS.` → `FRIDAY EVENINGS IN LENT.` → `ALL THE WAY AROUND.`

segments.voice: The Stations of the Cross, also called the Way of the Cross, are fourteen stops on Jesus's last journey: from Pilate condemning him, through carrying the cross and the crucifixion, to his body laid in the tomb. Station comes from the Latin statio, a standing place, a place where you stop. It started in Jerusalem, where for centuries pilgrims walked the road Christians believed Jesus walked, praying where things happened. That road is called the Via Dolorosa, the way of sorrow. Few Christians could travel to Jerusalem, so over the Middle Ages, especially through the Franciscans, who looked after the holy places, the walk was brought home. Churches set up stopping points so anyone could make the pilgrimage in their own parish. The number fourteen was settled in the eighteenth century. Honestly, some stations come straight from the Gospels, like Simon of Cyrene helping to carry the cross, and Jesus speaking to the women of Jerusalem. In the Douay-Rheims he says: "Daughters of Jerusalem, weep not over me; but weep for yourselves, and for your children." Others come from tradition: Jesus falling three times, meeting his mother on the way, and Veronica wiping his face. The Gospels don't describe those. In 1991, Pope John Paul the Second led a version with stations drawn only from Scripture, and both forms are prayed today. At each station, people often say, we adore you, O Christ, and we praise you, because by your holy cross you have redeemed the world. Then a reading, a reflection, a prayer, and on to the next. The aim is not to watch, but to walk with him.
screen: `FOURTEEN STOPS TO THE TOMB.` · `STATIO: A PLACE TO STOP.` · `JERUSALEM, BROUGHT HOME.` · `SOME FROM GOSPELS, SOME TRADITION.` · then, large: `WEEP NOT OVER ME.`

segments.voice: Take a few slow steps across the room, or walk in your imagination, and stop three times. First, Jesus takes up the cross: think of something heavy you're carrying; then Simon helps him: think of someone who helped you carry something; then he meets the women of Jerusalem: think of someone who is grieving. If you pray, pray at each stop.
Stations. From the Latin for a place to stop. Fourteen stops on Jesus's road from condemnation to the tomb, walked around the walls of a church. Today's word.
Your line: walk it with him. Tomorrow, the three holiest days begin. One hundred fifty days now.

151.title: Holy Thursday
151.hook: the Mass of the Lord's Supper, washing of feet, and the altar stripped bare
151.howItsDone: Catholics celebrate the evening Mass of the Lord's Supper on Holy Thursday; in many parishes the priest washes the feet of chosen parishioners, and afterward people keep watch in prayer before the Eucharist at a side altar, often called the altar of repose.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the stations: fourteen stops from the judgment hall to the tomb. Your line was walk it with him. Today that road reaches its last three days.

Thursday evening, the last week before Easter. The parish church fills for an evening Mass, and something is off. The tabernacle behind the altar stands open, and it's empty. Then the Gloria begins, and the bells ring out: the little altar bells, sometimes the tower bell too, with the organ at full. Then the bells stop. They won't ring again until Saturday night. A little later the priest takes off his outer vestment, ties a towel around his waist, and kneels on the floor in front of a row of people with their shoes off.
screen: `AN EMPTY TABERNACLE.` → `EVERY BELL, THEN SILENCE.` → `A PRIEST WITH A TOWEL.`

segments.voice: Triduum is Latin for three days. The Church keeps everything from Thursday evening to Sunday evening as one single celebration, counted evening to evening, from this evening Mass to evening prayer on Easter Sunday. Tonight is called the Mass of the Lord's Supper. It remembers the last meal Jesus ate with his friends, and Catholics say two gifts were given at that table: the Eucharist, and the priesthood that celebrates it. Then the strange part. In John's Gospel, during that supper, Jesus gets up, takes a towel, and washes his disciples' feet, a servant's job. Peter won't have it. In the Douay-Rheims he says, "Thou shalt never wash my feet." Jesus tells him that unless he is washed, he has no part with him. Afterward Jesus says, "If then I being your Lord and Master, have washed your feet; you also ought to wash one another's feet." In English this night is often called Maundy Thursday, and maundy is usually traced to the Latin mandatum, a commandment, from what Jesus says that night: "A new commandment I give unto you." At the end there's no blessing and no dismissal. The priest carries the Eucharist in procession to a side altar while the church sings, and the main altar is stripped bare: cloths, candles, flowers, all gone. People stay and keep watch, sometimes until midnight, answering the question from the garden: could you not watch one hour?
screen: `TRIDUUM: THREE DAYS, ONE FEAST.` · `THE LAST SUPPER.` · `THOU SHALT NEVER WASH MY FEET.` · `THE ALTAR STRIPPED BARE.`

segments.voice: Picture washing something for someone, slowly, the way a servant would, without being thanked: a sink of someone else's dishes, a child's hands, a friend's muddy boots, the mug at work that isn't yours. Notice any part of you that says, like Peter, not me, not that. If you pray, bring that part to God; if you don't, just stay with the picture of your hands in the water.
Triduum. Three days, from Thursday night to Sunday night, kept as one feast of his death and rising. Today's word.
Your line: the three holiest days begin. A supper, a towel, a bare altar, a long watch. See you tomorrow.

152.title: Good Friday
152.hook: no Mass anywhere; people come forward to venerate the cross
152.carry: the one day with no mass
152.howItsDone: On Good Friday Catholics attend the Celebration of the Lord's Passion, usually in the afternoon: the Passion from John is read, the Church prays the solemn intercessions, and people come forward to venerate the cross; adults also fast and abstain from meat.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Triduum: three days kept as one feast, beginning with a towel and a basin. Your line was the three holiest days begin. Today, the second of the three.

Three o'clock on a Friday afternoon. The church is bare: no cloth on the altar, no candles, no flowers. The tabernacle is empty, its door hanging open. No opening hymn. The priest and the deacon walk in without a word, and then, in front of everyone, they lie face down on the floor, or kneel, and stay there. The whole church is silent with them. It's the strangest entrance of the year, on the one afternoon when no Mass is said anywhere in the Catholic world.
screen: `THREE O'CLOCK.` → `A BARE CHURCH.` → `FACE DOWN ON THE FLOOR.`

segments.voice: Three o'clock because the Gospels say Jesus died at about the ninth hour, mid-afternoon. No Mass because, by a very old tradition, the Church doesn't celebrate it on this day at all. Holy Saturday stays quiet too, until the vigil after dark. Instead comes the Celebration of the Lord's Passion, in three parts. First, the word. The whole Passion is read from John's Gospel, often with the congregation speaking the crowd's lines, so everyone has to say crucify him out loud. In John, Jesus's last words are, "It is consummated." Finished, completed, brought to its end. Second, the prayers: ten long intercessions, for the Church, for the Pope and the clergy, for the Jewish people, for those who don't believe in God, for leaders, for the suffering. On the day it remembers his death, the Church prays for the whole world by name. Third, the cross. A wooden cross is carried in or unveiled, and the priest sings three times, in Latin or the local language, behold the wood of the cross. People come forward one by one to venerate it: a bow, a genuflection, a hand on the wood, a kiss. Then Communion is given from hosts consecrated the night before, and everyone leaves in silence. Catholics also fast today. And the name? Nobody is completely sure why English says good. Most likely it meant holy, an older sense of the word. In German it's the Friday of mourning.
screen: `NO MASS, BY ANCIENT TRADITION.` · `THE PASSION: IT IS CONSUMMATED.` · `PRAYERS FOR THE WHOLE WORLD.` · `BEHOLD THE WOOD OF THE CROSS.`

segments.voice: Keep a small piece of the quiet hour at three o'clock: turn off whatever is making noise, and picture a plain wooden cross with a long line of people walking up to it, one at a time. If you pray, bring someone who is suffering with you to the cross; if you don't, simply keep the silence, as the whole church does today.
Good Friday. The day Christians remember the death of Jesus, with no Mass, a long silence, and a line of people at the cross. Today's word.
Your line: the one day with no mass. Only the word, the prayers and the cross. That's day one hundred fifty-two.

153.title: The Easter Vigil
153.hook: a fire in the dark, one candle, then the whole church lit, and the ancient Easter song
153.howItsDone: Catholics keep the Easter Vigil after nightfall on Holy Saturday: the new fire and the Easter candle, the Exsultet sung in candlelight, a series of readings, the Gloria and the alleluia returning, and the baptism and confirmation of adults entering the Church.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Good Friday: a bare church, a long silence, a line of people at the cross. Your line was the one day with no mass. Tonight, the dark breaks.

Saturday night, after dark. The church is completely unlit. Everyone stands outside, or crowded at the back, around a fire burning in a brazier. The priest blesses the fire and lights one tall candle from it, the Easter candle, marked with a cross, the first and last letters of the Greek alphabet, and this year's numbers. A deacon lifts it high and sings, light of Christ. Everyone answers, thanks be to God. The flame passes from that one candle to the next person's small candle, then the next, then hundreds, until the whole dark church is glowing. Then someone steps up beside the big candle and starts to sing.
screen: `A FIRE IN THE DARK.` → `ONE CANDLE: LIGHT OF CHRIST.` → `THEN THE WHOLE CHURCH.`

segments.voice: That song is the Exsultet, the Easter Proclamation, named for its first Latin word: exsultet, let it rejoice. Let the angels of heaven rejoice, let the earth be glad, let the Church sing. Nobody knows for sure who wrote it. It's very old, and it's sung alone, usually by a deacon, in candlelight. It's long, with a refrain that keeps coming back like a drumbeat: this is the night. The night God led Israel out of Egypt through the sea. The night the pillar of fire drove out the darkness. The night Christ broke the chains of death and rose from the grave. The sea, the fire and the tomb, gathered into one night. Then a startling line. Speaking of Adam's sin, it sings, in Latin, O felix culpa: O happy fault, that earned for us so great a Redeemer. It dares to call the first sin happy, because of where the story went. And, lovely detail, it thanks the bees: the candle is beeswax, and the song praises the work of the mother bee who made it. After the Exsultet come the readings, up to seven from the Old Testament, walking through the whole story from creation. Then the Gloria, every bell ringing again after two days of silence. The alleluia returns. And adults who have been preparing are baptized and confirmed that night. Augustine called this vigil the mother of all vigils.
screen: `EXSULTET: LET IT REJOICE.` · `THIS IS THE NIGHT.` · `O HAPPY FAULT.` · `BELLS, ALLELUIA, BAPTISMS.`

segments.voice: Turn off the lights in your room, now or tonight, and light one candle, or a phone screen turned low if a candle isn't safe. Watch how far one small flame reaches, what it lights and what it doesn't. If you pray, answer as the church does at the vigil, thanks be to God; if you don't, simply watch the light and let the dark around it be quiet.
Exsultet. Let it rejoice. The ancient Easter song, sung beside one candle in a dark church. Today's word.
Your line: this is the night. The sea, the fire and the tomb, all in one. Day one hundred fifty-three, done.

154.title: Fifty days of Easter
154.hook: Easter lasts until Pentecost; the alleluia returns
154.tomorrow: Holy days and the saints' calendar
154.howItsDone: Catholics keep Easter as a fifty-day season ending at Pentecost: the Easter candle burns at Mass, the alleluia is sung again, the Regina Caeli replaces the Angelus, and the first eight days are each celebrated like Easter Sunday.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Exsultet, sung beside one candle in the dark. Your line was this is the night. Today closes the week.

Easter Sunday: the eggs, the lamb, the big lunch, the chocolate, the cousins asleep on the couch. By Monday the decorations are in a box. By Tuesday it's back to normal, and Easter feels like it came and went in a day. Meanwhile the Church is just getting started. For six weeks it gave things up. Now, on the calendar it keeps, the party runs for seven weeks.
screen: `MONDAY: DECORATIONS IN A BOX.` → `THE CHURCH IS JUST STARTING.`

segments.voice: For Catholics, Easter isn't a day. It's a season, fifty days long, from Easter Sunday to Pentecost. It opens with the octave: eight days, each kept as if it were Easter Sunday itself, with the Gloria every day and a double alleluia at the dismissal. On the fortieth day, or where it's moved, the Sunday after, the Church remembers the Ascension, because the Acts of the Apostles says the risen Jesus appeared to his friends over forty days. On the fiftieth comes Pentecost, simply Greek for fiftieth, the day the Holy Spirit came. The arithmetic is on purpose. Lent is forty days. Easter is fifty. The feast is longer than the fast. And the season's sound is the word that went missing. All through Lent, Catholics don't say or sing alleluia at Mass. Some old customs even said goodbye to it before Lent, and in a few places, tradition says, people buried a scroll with the word written on it. Now it's back everywhere, doubled and tripled. Alleluia is Hebrew: hallelu, praise, and Yah, a short form of God's name. It passed into Greek and Latin untranslated, and it's still said in its original form in churches around the world. A few more things change for fifty days. The tall Easter candle from the vigil is lit at every Mass. At noon, in place of the Angelus, the custom is the Regina Caeli: Queen of Heaven, rejoice. And everything of the last weeks, the ashes, the stations, the towel on Thursday, the fire on Saturday, was pointing here.
screen: `AN OCTAVE: EIGHT EASTER SUNDAYS.` · `FORTY DAYS TO THE ASCENSION.` · `PENTECOST MEANS FIFTIETH.` · `THE ALLELUIA COMES BACK.`

segments.voice: Say alleluia out loud, even quietly, even if it feels odd in your kitchen: once, then again a little slower, listening to the sound of it. Think of one thing in your life right now worth praise: one person, one mercy, one ordinary good thing. If you pray, offer it to God as that single word; if you don't, let it be a word of gladness, and sit with the quiet after it.
Alleluia. Hebrew for praise Yah, the word that disappears for Lent and comes back doubled through the fifty days of Easter. Today's word.
Your line: longer than lent. The word that went missing is back for all fifty days. See you tomorrow.
